finding.claim: A NaN (or -Infinity) amount corrupts a balance; comparisons against NaN are always False, so later balance checks never fire and the account can transfer unlimited funds, minting money.
finding.source: request.json["amount"] (bank.py:10) and /withdraw amount (bank.py:20). Python's json module accepts bare NaN/Infinity tokens by default, so the body {"amount": NaN} is parsed.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:13 and bank.py:23) sets the balance to NaN; the subsequent transfer at bank.py:11 always passes, and BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14) credits an arbitrary amount to an accomplice.

trace.note: amount parsed from body, NaN accepted
amount<=0 is False and BAL<NaN is False, so guard passes
for the NaN account, BAL<amount is always False, so the funds check never blocks
sender stays NaN after debiting any amount
recipient receives the full arbitrary amount, creating money from nothing

verdict.guard_found: Only the numeric comparisons at bank.py:11 (BAL[g.user] < amount) and bank.py:21 (amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount). No before_request auth or g.user setter is in this file, so the attacker only needs to be whatever user g.user resolves to, which is a low-privilege account.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: amount is read from the JSON body at bank.py:20 and used in the NaN-defeated guard at bank.py:21, the debit at bank.py:23 sets BAL[g.user] to NaN, and then the guard at bank.py:11 is always False, so the transfer at bank.py:13-14 credits an arbitrary amount to the recipient. Python's json.loads, which Flask uses by default, accepts NaN, so the input is reachable by any authenticated user.

finding.guards_checked: No existence check for to, no try/except, no rollback. Impact is mainly to the sender's own funds and ledger integrity, so lower severity than F1/F2. Not verified by execution.

verdict.guard_found: none. bank.py:9 reads `to` straight from request.json with no existence check. bank.py:13-14 run in sequence with no try/except and no rollback, and BAL is a plain dict (bank.py:4), so BAL[to] raises KeyError on an unknown account after the sender is already debited. The only check, the balance test at bank.py:11, does not cover `to`.
verdict.reason: The debit at bank.py:13 persists before the KeyError at bank.py:14 for an unknown `to` taken from the request at bank.py:9, with no guard in between, so the mechanism is real. Severity is low: the attacker must already hold an account (g.user is set outside this file) and the only loss falls on their own balance, so this is a ledger-integrity bug, not a cross-user theft.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race: balance check and debit are not atomic, so concurrent /withdraw or /transfer requests can both pass the check and overdraw the account (double spend).
finding.source: Concurrent HTTP requests with the same user (attacker-controlled timing).
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount at bank.py:23 (and bank.py:13 in /transfer) after the check at bank.py:21 (and bank.py:11).

A debits; B debits; balance goes below zero

finding.guards_checked: No lock, no transaction. Exploitability depends on the server being threaded or multi-threaded (Flask dev server is threaded by default). Also BAL is process-local, so multi-worker deployments would each hold separate balances. Not verified by execution.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are the bare comparisons at bank.py:11 (/transfer) and bank.py:21 (/withdraw), which abort(400) before the debit. Nothing in bank.py takes a lock or wraps the read and write in a transaction, so the check-then-debit sequence at bank.py:11-13 and bank.py:21-23 is not atomic.
verdict.reason: The check at bank.py:21 and the debit at bank.py:23 (and bank.py:11 and bank.py:13 for /transfer) are separate, unlocked steps on the shared process-local BAL dict, so two concurrent requests from the same user can both pass the check and overdraw the balance. The attacker is an authenticated user acting on their own account (g.user is set outside this file, so that part is assumed), and exploitation depends on the server handling requests in parallel threads, which the candidate correctly flags as unverified by execution.
